title: Seastone Systems - Concurrency & Streaming Matrix Discovery
summary: Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private for low-latency streaming use cases. Primary goals: p95 < 180ms for short chat prompts, sustained 800-1200 concurrent streaming sessions, token/sec burst up to ~6k tokens/sec aggregate. Concerned about cold starts, KV cache warming, and data residency for EU. Wants benchmark plan and pilot with sample prompt set.
next_steps: Redwood to share benchmark worksheet and pilot run template by 2026-09-08
Customer to provide representative prompt set and traffic pattern by 2026-09-09
Schedule on-prem demo week of 2026-09-14 if private deployment pursued
action_items: Maya Chen - send hosted vs dedicated pricing grid + pilot terms - due 2026-09-08
Omar Siddiqui - propose benchmark plan (token/sec tests, streaming p95, KV warmup) - due 2026-09-07
Lena Martinez - share sanitized prompt corpus and traffic sketch - due 2026-09-09
header:
Date: 2026-09-05 16:00 UTC
Duration: 43 minutes
Recording: yes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE); Omar Siddiqui (Redwood SE); Lena Martinez (Seastone Head of ML); Raj Patel (Seastone Platform Eng); Sofia Gomez (Seastone CTO)
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro - I'm Maya, AE on the Redwood inference team, and with me is Omar, our systems SE.
[00:08] Omar Siddiqui: Hi all.
[00:10] Lena Martinez: Hi Maya, Omar. This is Lena, I run ML at Seastone. Sofia and Raj are also on.
[00:15] Sofia Gomez: Hey.
[00:17] Raj Patel: Hi.
[00:20] Maya Chen: Great. Goal for today is to understand your latency and throughput targets for streaming chat and figure out hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs. Happy to dig into numbers and a benchmark plan.
[00:28] Lena Martinez: Awesome. To be blunt, our product is real-time summarization for financial feeds. We need streaming tokens emitted to clients with p95 latency under about 150-180ms for short prompts — when it's just a 20-60 token reply. And then we have burst windows during market open where concurrent streaming sessions hit 800 to 1.2k.
[00:45] Omar Siddiqui: Okay, that helps. Do you have an average tokens/sec per session during those bursts?
[00:50] Lena Martinez: On average it's small, 8-12 tokens/sec per session, but bursts can spike when some customers request long history expands and we get higher token rates. Across the fleet we estimate aggregate bursts of up to ~6k tokens/sec for short periods.
[01:05] Maya Chen: Got it. Two dimensions here: per-session p95 and aggregate throughput. For p95 we usually look at model selection, serving runtime config (batching/window), and streaming path. For aggregate bursts, Dedicated gives predictable capacity but hosted can also absorb with autoscale if you accept some fallback policies.
[01:25] Raj Patel: What's the typical cold-start impact? If a request hits an idle shard, do we see big p95 tail spikes? That's a huge worry for us.
[01:33] Omar Siddiqui: Cold starts vary by model and quantization — warm KV cache matters. With our prefix caching and KV prewarm we can keep the p95 tail tight for most flows; cold start spikes happen primarily on model swap or an idle pool node. For hosted we have warm pools and fast spin-up, but dedicated is the lowest variance.
[01:50] Lena Martinez: When you say warm pools, is that an extra cost? We would need cost numbers compared to dedicated.
[01:55] Maya Chen: Yes, warm pools or reserved instances are billed. We'll send a pricing grid. Usually customers weigh the cost of warm capacity against the business cost of p95 breaches.
[02:05] Sofia Gomez: We also have EU data residency constraints for some customers. If we go hosted, can you guarantee the data stays in region and is audited?
[02:13] Maya Chen: We support region routing and have audit logs, SOC2, and SSO integrations. For stricter residency or air-gapped needs, Private deployment (VPC / on-prem) is the option. We can also do dedicated capacity pinned in an EU region.
[02:28] Raj Patel: From a performance standpoint, how does dedicated differ for streaming latency?
[02:32] Omar Siddiqui: Dedicated gives you pinned GPU pools which eliminates noisy neighbor effects and reduces scheduling latency. It also allows us to tune kernel selection and batching aggressively for your request patterns. For streaming, that often translates to 10-40% lower p95 in practice depending on model.
[02:48] Lena Martinez: Do you have examples or benchmarks? We're particularly sensitive to the early tokens — token 1-5 latency.
[02:55] Omar Siddiqui: We do. I'll share a benchmark worksheet. Example: on a 7B-ish encoder-decoder streaming model, with continuous batching disabled for token-by-token streaming, we've seen p95s around 120ms on dedicated hardware for 20–40 token responses. Hosted varies but with warmed pools we can target ~140–180ms. Your prompt shapes will matter a lot.
[03:20] Speaker 1: (unintelligible)
[03:22] Lena Martinez: Okay. We run a hybrid: most traffic is short replies but some internal analytics spawn long-form synthesis that squeezes throughput. Could caching help?
[03:30] Omar Siddiqui: Yes, prefix/KV caching can cut token cost and reduce inference time for repeated prefixes. But it depends on how repeatable your prompts are. You mentioned long history expands — we can cache the history embeddings or KV to speed up subsequent tokens.
[03:44] Raj Patel: How does streaming interplay with batching? We want low latency but also throughput efficiency.
[03:49] Maya Chen: Streaming and batching are a tradeoff. For pure streaming low-latency token emission we often configure minimal batching (or continuous small batches). For cost efficiency during steady state we use adaptive batching and KV caching. Redwood Optimize can propose batching windows tuned to your p95 SLOs.
[04:05] Lena Martinez: About quantization — we plan to use 4-bit quantized models in production. Does that change p95 or throughput significantly?
[04:12] Omar Siddiqui: Quantization helps memory and throughput, but it can slightly affect latency per token depending on kernel paths. Our runtime has quantization-friendly execution; most customers see improved throughput and similar or slightly better p95s because you can fit more concurrency on the same GPU. We'll include model-specific profiles in the benchmark sheet.
[04:30] Sofia Gomez: On security: KMS integration, audit trail, SSO — do you support customer-managed keys in Private?
[04:36] Maya Chen: Yes. Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM and full audit logs. Dedicated in a VPC can also be configured with KMS boundaries if you need that.
[04:46] Raj Patel: Network egress costs from EU region are a concern. Do you help with region routing to minimize cross-region hops?
[04:52] Maya Chen: We do region-based routing policies and can pin traffic to EU-hosted models/lakes. We'll capture your regions in the pilot.
[05:00] Lena Martinez: About the benchmark: what do you need from us?
[05:03] Omar Siddiqui: Representative prompt corpus (sanitized), session concurrency profile (ramp patterns at open/close), desired SLOs (p95 target, allowed error-rate), and whether to include long-form synthesis flows.
[05:13] Lena Martinez: We'll share a sanitized sample and a traffic sketch.
[05:16] Maya Chen: Great. Suggested pilot: 1) baseline hosted run with warmed pools, measure p95 for your short prompts; 2) dedicated baseline on similar model family; 3) stress tests for token/sec bursts and KV warmup; 4) streaming token-by-token profiling. We'll provide scripts and a worksheet.
[05:34] Sofia Gomez: Timeline? We need results before our Q4 launch planning.
[05:38] Maya Chen: We'll aim to deliver a benchmark plan within 48 hours and execute pilot in ~2 weeks after we receive artifacts.
[05:44] Raj Patel: Are there fallback options if dedicated capacity dips or we exceed concurrency? For hosted, can you fallback to a smaller model or queued routing?
[05:51] Omar Siddiqui: Yes, we have policy-based routing and automatic fallback to compatible model variants or burst capacity. Fallbacks are configurable by latency tiers and cost tiers.
[06:00] Lena Martinez: One more: How do you measure token/sec aggregate across shards? We need a number we can align to for cost planning.
[06:05] Omar Siddiqui: We'll instrument per-shard token/sec and aggregate over windows; the benchmark worksheet will show expected tokens/sec per GPU shape and concurrency mapping. That will let us estimate cost per million tokens for your workload.
[06:18] Speaker 2: (laughs)
[06:20] Lena Martinez: Sounds good. I do have one worry: SLOs are enforced by product teams — how often do you see SLO regressions when moving from hosted pilot to dedicated?
[06:28] Maya Chen: Rare — most regressions come from model changes or prompt drift. Our rollout controls (canary, A/B) and regression alerts tied to prompt sets help catch those early.
[06:38] Sofia Gomez: OK. That helps.
[06:40] Maya Chen: Recap and action items: we'll send the benchmark worksheet and pricing grid (hosted vs dedicated), Omar will draft the test plan, Lena will share the prompt set and traffic pattern. We'll target the pilot kickoff week of Sep 14.
[06:55] Raj Patel: Thanks everyone.
[06:57] Lena Martinez: Thank you.
[07:00] Maya Chen: Thanks, we'll follow up by email with the worksheet and next steps.
[07:05] (meeting ends)
